title: Betting on electric cars before it was popular
problem: Electric cars were seen as slow, costly niche products.
innovation: Build premium electric cars first, then move to cheaper models.
overview: Tesla is an electric vehicle and energy company founded in 2003.
model: Sells vehicles directly to customers and also sells energy products.
technology: Batteries, electric motors and vehicle software.
milestones: First car, the Roadster, begins deliveries
advantages: Early focus on batteries and software
challenges: Building cars at scale is hard and capital-intensive
lesson: Start with a small premium market, learn, then expand to a larger one.
future: Cheaper batteries could affect transport and energy storage. This is an open question, not a prediction.

title: From graphics chips to AI computing
problem: Graphics chips were used mainly for games.
innovation: Make GPUs programmable for general computing with CUDA.
overview: NVIDIA designs chips and software. It was founded in 1993.
model: Designs chips and sells chips, systems and software.
technology: GPUs and the CUDA programming platform.
milestones: GeForce 256 marketed as the first GPU
challenges: Depends on outside manufacturers; competition and export rules
lesson: Software tools can make hardware much more valuable.
future: Demand for AI computing may shape chip design. This is uncertain.

title: Making rockets reusable
problem: Rockets were thrown away after one launch, which is costly.
overview: SpaceX is a space launch company founded in 2002.
model: Sells launch services and runs a satellite internet service.
milestones: Dragon docked with the International Space Station
Crewed Dragon flight carried NASA astronauts to the ISS
advantages: Reuse can lower the cost of launches
lesson: Repeated testing and learning from failures can solve hard problems.
future: Cheaper launch could make more space projects practical. This is uncertain.

title: From DVDs by mail to streaming
problem: Renting movies meant going to a store and paying late fees.
innovation: Rent DVDs by mail with no late fees, then move to streaming over the internet.
overview: Netflix is an entertainment company founded in 1997.
model: Customers pay a regular subscription to watch content.
technology: Internet video streaming and recommendation software.
challenges: Competition from many other streaming services
Content is costly to produce or license
lesson: Be ready to change your own business when technology changes.
future: Internet speed and devices keep changing how people watch. How it will end up is uncertain.

title: Selling computing power as a service
problem: Starting a website or app meant buying and running your own servers.
innovation: Rent computing and storage over the internet and pay only for what you use.
overview: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the cloud computing business of Amazon.
model: Customers pay for usage of computing, storage and other services.
technology: Large data centres and software that shares them among many customers.
challenges: Strong competition from other cloud providers
Customers worry about outages and costs
lesson: A tool built for your own needs can become a product for others.
lessons: Lower the cost of starting for others
future: More software may run in the cloud. The exact path is uncertain.

title: From a college website to a family of apps
problem: People wanted an easy way to stay in touch with friends and family online.
innovation: A social network that grew from one campus to the whole world, then added photo, messaging and VR products.
overview: Meta Platforms owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and VR products. Facebook was started in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg and others.
model: Free apps for users. The company earns mainly by showing ads.
technology: Social networking software, large-scale data systems, AI recommendations, and virtual and augmented reality.
advantages: Very large user base across several apps
challenges: Concerns about privacy and harmful content
Regulators in many countries are watching it closely
Its VR and metaverse bets are long-term and uncertain
lesson: Buying or building products that people use daily can make a company strong, but trust and privacy must be earned.
lessons: Network effects: more users make an app more useful
Ads can fund free products, but people care about their data
Do not depend on one product
future: VR, AR and AI may change how people connect. Whether people will adopt them widely is uncertain.

title: Organising the world's information
problem: The early web was hard to search; finding useful pages was slow and unreliable.
innovation: A search engine that ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them (PageRank), later expanded into many products.
overview: Google was founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin while they were students at Stanford. It is now part of Alphabet.
model: Most revenue comes from advertising shown on search and other products. It also sells cloud services.
technology: Search ranking, large data centres, Android, machine learning and cloud computing.
milestones: Alphabet created as a parent company
Google researchers published the Transformer paper, behind many modern AI models
advantages: Huge amounts of data and computing power
Products used by billions of people
challenges: Antitrust and regulatory cases in several countries
New AI products compete with search
lesson: Solve one clear problem very well, then use that trust to build many products.
lessons: Free tools can build large audiences
future: AI may change how people search and find answers. How this will play out is uncertain.

title: Bringing AI chat to everyone
problem: Powerful AI research was mostly used by experts and hard for ordinary people to try.
innovation: A simple chat tool, ChatGPT, that let anyone talk to a large language model in plain language.
overview: OpenAI is an AI research and product company. It was founded in December 2015.
model: Offers free and paid plans for its AI tools, and sells access to developers and companies.
technology: Large language models trained on very large amounts of text, and large-scale computing.
milestones: Created a capped-profit company alongside its non-profit
advantages: Early lead in popular AI chat products
Close ties to large computing partners
challenges: Training and running AI costs a lot
Debates over safety, copyright and how the company is governed
lesson: A simple interface can bring a hard technology to millions of people.
lessons: Make the product easy to try
Research and product need each other
New technology brings new rules and debates
future: AI assistants may become part of many jobs and tools. Their limits and rules are still being worked out.

title: Making mobile internet cheap in India
problem: Mobile data in India was costly and slow for many people.
innovation: A 4G-only network with very low data prices and free voice calls, launched at scale.
overview: Reliance Jio is an Indian telecom company, part of Reliance Industries. It launched its commercial services in September 2016.
model: Sells mobile data and phone plans, plus digital services built on top of the network.
technology: A network built on 4G and voice over LTE, with a large investment in towers and fibre.
milestones: Commercial launch with a free introductory offer
JioPhone announced for people moving from basic phones
Jio Platforms attracted outside investors, including Facebook and Google
advantages: Built on new technology from day one
Low prices attracted many first-time internet users
challenges: Building a network needs very large investment
Price competition with other telecom firms
lesson: A big drop in price can unlock a whole new group of users.
lessons: Build for the market's biggest gap
Use the network to launch other services
future: Cheap data helped digital payments, video and apps grow in India. What comes next with 5G is uncertain.

title: Simple messaging for everyone
problem: Texting by SMS was costly and different between countries.
innovation: A simple app that sends messages over the internet, on any phone, with no ads.
overview: WhatsApp was founded in 2009 by Jan Koum and Brian Acton. Facebook (now Meta) announced it was buying WhatsApp in 2014.
model: Early on, a small yearly fee in some countries. Today the app is free and the company is exploring business tools.
technology: Messaging over the internet and end-to-end encryption.
milestones: End-to-end encryption rolled out to all chats
advantages: Works on many phones and in low-bandwidth places
challenges: Fake news and misinformation can spread fast
lesson: Doing one simple job very well can win billions of users.
future: Messaging apps may become places for shopping, payments and customer service. This is still developing.
